## Statement

Source IPD can identify the omitted variable's outcome association in the arm it observes, but with one treatment per study the data cannot decompose that slope into a treatment-invariant prognostic component and treatment-specific modification, cannot identify the comparator-arm slope, and cannot establish that either transports to the comparator study or the decision target. A sensitivity analysis that imports such a coefficient, or a prevalence or correlation taken from an external registry or clinical study report, therefore carries a second untestable transport assumption of its own. Ren et al. 2025 (doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.13) do exactly this and concede the analysis may be biased if the assumed values for the unmeasured confounders differ from those observed in the IPD study, offering expert elicitation and external-data regression as remedies whose own transport is untested.

## Why it is open

The observed data do not update a nonidentified bias parameter, so whether a coefficient borrowed from the source IPD or an external registry holds in the comparator study or the decision target is untestable within the analysis, and nothing in current practice flags that the sensitivity parameter has its own identification problem. Non-transportability bites hardest exactly where it matters, when the omitted variable modifies the treatment effect or proxies for care setting, and the standard shortcut of importing one source-arm prognostic coefficient into both potential outcomes quietly assumes that it does not. External sources come from different populations, eras, care pathways and measurement systems, and assessing whether a bias parameter transports would require the same unavailable joint information the QBA was meant to supply, while access to registries, clinical study reports and companion-trial IPD is often restricted.

## What has been tried

::: {.table-scroll}

| Work | What it contributes |
|---|---|
| [Ren et al. 2025, Research Synthesis Methods](https://doi.org/10.1017/rsm.2025.13) | Fixes the outcome association of the omitted covariate from the IPD source and assumes it applies in the comparator population, conceding the result may be biased if the assumed means for the unmeasured confounders differ from the observed IPD values, and proposing elicitation and external-data regression whose transport is untested. |

:::

## Probable solution or research direction

Report the transport of each sensitivity parameter as an assumption rather than attempting to validate it with a diagnostic built from the same data, and state explicitly which parameters are source-estimated and which are assumed. Parameterize treatment-specific and study-specific associations for the omitted variable with explicit variable-by-treatment interaction terms and report results across a range of assumed modification instead of assuming a purely prognostic omitted variable. Treat externally sourced parameters as estimates carrying their own exchangeability assumption, widening ranges to reflect transport uncertainty or moving to partial identification rather than importing a point value.

## Verification

::: {.verification-trail}
**Verdict.** Partially addressed. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced. Reopened by the full-text reading: 1 finding from 1 paper survived both the reader and an independent second reviewer, so the verdict moves from confirmed-open to partially-addressed, on a single finding.

**The source said.** "An omitted-variable outcome association estimated in the source study, or a prevalence or correlation taken from an external registry or clinical study report, is imported into the target as if it transported, so the sensitivity analysis carries a second untestable transport assumption of its own. In an unanchored design with one treatment per study the primary data also cannot separate a study effect, a prognostic effect of the omitted variable and treatment-effect modification by it."

**What was wrong with it.** GPT-5.6 Sol narrowed the identification claim: a study intercept cannot generally mimic a within-source slope for the omitted variable, so a study effect, a prognostic effect and effect modification are not all equally indistinguishable. Importing one coefficient into both potential outcomes is a valid scenario under an explicit no-effect-modification and transport assumption rather than an error, and the entry's proposal to build transportability diagnostics for bias parameters cannot work as stated, because no diagnostic using the same primary data can test equality of an unobserved target association. The entry cited nothing; the literature auditor supplied Ren et al. 2025 (doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.13).

**Revised by the full-text reading.** Applied 2026-07-26 full-text reading of the consolidated library (687 papers).

Verdict changed
:   **confirmed-open -> partially-addressed** 1 surviving finding from: Sensitivity analysis for an unobserved moderator in RCT-to-t. New citations: 10.1214/16-AOAS1001

Literature and prior-art check
:   **open / supported.** No prior_work is given, but claims 1 to 6 are corroborated by primary sources I retrieved. Ren et al. 2025 fix the outcome association of the omitted covariate from the IPD source and simply assume it applies in the comparator population; they concede the resulting analysis 'may be biased, particularly when the sample size is small, if the assumed mean values for the unmeasured confounders differ significantly from the observed values in the IPD study', and their proposed remedies (expert elicitation, external-data regression prediction) are all extrapolations whose transport is untested. Claim 4 is a structural identification fact for the one-treatment-per-study layout and is correct. Claims 7 to 9 are the open part: claim 9 ('no accepted procedure for assessing whether a bias parameter transports') is a no-method-exists assertion; my searches found transportability diagnostics for treatment effects but none for bias parameters, so I treat claim 9 as unfalsified rather than positively verified. Note that a structurally untestable transport assumption for a nonidentified parameter cannot be resolved by any paper, so this entry should remain open indefinitely and be framed as a reporting requirement rather than a solvable estimation problem.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens
:   **open / overstated.** C1, C5, C7, and C8 are correct. If U is measured and varies in source IPD, that study can estimate its arm-specific U-outcome association. With one treatment per study, the data cannot decompose that source slope into a treatment-invariant prognostic component and treatment-specific modification, identify the comparator-arm slope, or separate treatment and study main effects. C4 is therefore too broad: a study intercept cannot generally mimic a within-source U slope, so all three quantities are not equally indistinguishable. C3 is also conditional rather than mandatory; importing one coefficient is a valid sensitivity scenario under an explicit no-effect-modification and transport assumption, while treatment-specific parameters are needed to relax it. C2 and C6 depend on estimand and scale; on non-collapsible scales even a purely prognostic covariate distribution can change the marginal contrast. External sources can inform but not validate transport. C9 is a literature-exhaustiveness claim outside this lens, and no diagnostic using the same primary data can test equality of an unobserved target association. The open task is honest sensitivity or partial identification, not a diagnostic that creates identification.

Decision path
:   `R5:default-open → R9:substantiated-single-overstatement:codex`

:::

## How the evidence falls in time

5 papers in the reviewed corpus bear on this problem, published 2017 to 2025. Partial progress is on the record, and later work still calls this open. Both belong in view.

::: {.table-scroll}

| Year | Says | Paper |
|---|---|---|
| 2017 | partly addresses it | Sensitivity analysis for an unobserved moderator in RCT-to-target-population generalization of treatment effects (Nguyen, Ebnesajjad, Cole, Stuart; arXiv:1610.06943v1, published Annals of Applied Statistics 2017;11(1):225-247) |
| 2018 | confirms it is open | Sensitivity analyses for effect modifiers not observed in the target population when generalizing treatment effects from a randomized controlled trial: Assumptions, models, effect scales, data scenarios, and implementation details (Nguyen, Ackerman, Schmid, Cole, Stuart, PLoS ONE 2018;13(12):e0208795) |
| 2020 | confirms it is open | Performance of unanchored matching-adjusted indirect comparison (MAIC) for the evidence synthesis of single-arm trials with time-to-event outcomes |
| 2021 | confirms it is open | Applying Quantitative Bias Analysis to Epidemiologic Data, Second Edition (Fox, MacLehose, Lash; Springer, Statistics for Biology and Health, 2021) |
| 2025 | confirms it is open | Quantitative bias analysis for unmeasured confounding in unanchored population-adjusted indirect comparisons |

:::
